Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

mysterymodel 0.0.0.9000

First development version; nothing is released yet. This records the history by theme rather than by version. Each entry names the pull request that made the change and, where a question had to be settled rather than merely implemented, the record in inst/decisions.md that settled it.

The pipeline

  • mm_project(), mm_clean(), mm_eda(), mm_model(), mm_predict(), mm_validate(), mm_nomogram() and mm_synthetic_cohort() are the whole public surface. Everything else is internal (#1, #2, #3).
  • The public prefix is mm_ (#4, DEC-002).
  • mm_clean() returns a ledger that reconciles. Rows in must equal rows out plus every exclusion, and a mismatch is an error rather than a note, because a cohort count that cannot be reconciled against the raw export is the commonest reason a published flow diagram does not add up (#2).
  • mm_eda() carries the denominator each percentage is taken over and the missing count beside it, so a percentage computed over the complete rows cannot read as a fact about the cohort (#2).
  • mm_nomogram() reads the drawn nomogram back the way a clinician reads it and refuses to return one that disagrees with mm_predict() (#3).
  • Requires R 4.5 (#15). An exact patch-level dependency is not expressible: R CMD check --as-cran rejects R (>= 4.5.2).

Honest performance reporting

  • mm_validate() returns one row per basis, because apparent, bootstrap-corrected and held-out numbers are not interchangeable and presenting one as another is the commonest way a published model flatters itself (#3).
  • The fixed-model bootstrap is labelled as what rms::validate() does: it refits one formula and does not re-derive anything the formula was chosen by. mm_full_process() refits the whole strategy inside every resample and names what it re-executes (#3).
  • Clustered resampling draws whole patients when the project declares a cluster, including inside rms::validate(), which takes a cluster through predab.resample(). Resampling rows under a clustered design narrows every interval it touches (#9).
  • Resamples that rms could not fit are read off its n column and disclosed. Its own report of the shortfall is behind pr, which defaults off, so a corrected index could be an average over a self-selected subset with nothing on the object to say so (#9).
  • Apparent calibration is withheld rather than printed as 0 and 1. Scoring an unpenalized fit on its own rows forces both, so they describe the estimator and not the model. The identity is detected rather than assumed, so a penalized fit keeps its estimate (#10).
  • One scaled-Brier reference down the whole column, the development cohort’s own, because a column of scores against different references is a comparison a reader will make and should not (#11).
  • The c-statistic comes from the ROC and its bounds from the interval, which are two computations. Reading the estimate out of the middle of ci.auc() discarded a calculable c-statistic whenever DeLong could not be computed (#11).
  • Every interval names its method and the event and non-event counts it rests on, in a new non_events column. An interval that cannot be computed is NA with the reason; one of zero width, which is what DeLong returns on complete separation or complete ties, says so rather than reading as precision; a limit truncated at the edge of the parameter space is named a bound. A corrected c-statistic carries no interval and says why: that needs a nested bootstrap, which is not implemented (#19, DEC-006).

Refusing what cannot be meant

  • A predictor that reproduces the outcome, or its exact complement, is refused by mm_leakage(). Separation that is not duplication is reported instead, because in a small cohort it can be real. A strong but non-deterministic association is not mentioned at all (#13, DEC-004).
  • mm_check_resamples() refuses a fractional, missing, infinite or non-numeric resample count before any seed is set, rather than letting as.integer() turn 2.7 into 2 (#13, DEC-004).
  • mm_metrics() refuses a predicted probability outside [0, 1] rather than clamping it, because a clamped 1.5 becomes a plausible Brier score (#13, DEC-004).
  • Validating against a cohort that is not the one the model was fitted on is an error, checked by a hash of the modelling columns rather than a row count, and a reordering is refused too (#9).

Counting the sample that exists

  • Every reported count describes the rows rms fitted, not the rows it was handed. The sample-size gate judged the larger, partly imaginary sample, which made it most lenient exactly where data is most incomplete (#6).
  • Which rows are modelled is decided once, before fitting, and the datadist, the fit and the prediction schema are all built from that frame. Left to na.action the three disagreed, and a value no fitted row carried came back labelled as interpolation while the drawn nomogram reached axis values the model was never estimated on (#7).
  • mm_evaluable() is the one eligibility rule, read by fitting and by both kinds of validation. A missing predictor, a missing outcome and the overlap are counted apart, because taking a missing outcome for a non-event leaves the event count unchanged while inflating the denominator (#8, DEC-003).
  • A factor level carried only by dropped rows is removed and named in lost_levels, since rms answers one with a singular Hessian that identifies neither the variable nor the level (#7).

Patient data

  • The model carries no copy of the cohort. A formula keeps the environment it was built in and rms::lrm() stores that on fit$terms and fit$sformula, so a model built the default way held the whole cohort, patient identifiers included, into anything that saved it. The formula is built in baseenv() (#5). The fitted model went from 176.5 KB to 36.1 KB and 500 planted identifiers to none, with the coefficient fingerprint unchanged.
  • mm_predict() requires newdata, so no patient-level original is retained and no stored copy can drift from the data the caller has (#3).

Tests

  • 617 tests across 16 files, including 20 saboteurs that were each verified to fire against a deliberately disabled guard (#12), a leakage suite (#13), and a discrimination-interval suite that checks every degenerate case against an independent pROC call rather than a recorded number (#19).

Simplification

  • An audit for over-engineering produced thirteen findings; seven were implemented, one partly, and five retained on evidence (#16, #17, #18, DEC-005). pROC was kept because Hmisc::rcorr.cens() returns an interval where DeLong correctly reports that none is estimable, and the capability spike was kept because it still reproduces its matrix exactly. No reported number moved.
